A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same work, with matching authors, research problem, and principal methods. The main text, figures, table, equations, and Appendices A–C are available and support a reliable comparison.

before.justification: Section 5 and Figures 1–3 report original simulations comparing four clipped stochastic methods on synthetic variational inequalities, including distances averaged over twenty runs.

after.justification: Section 5 and Figures 1–4 report original simulations, including current-iterate and weighted-average-iterate results. The text retains averaging over twenty runs.

M1.justification: The proposed projection and Korpelevich update rules, sampling arrangements, and clipping formulas remain unchanged in Equations (7)–(9) and (16). Equation (18) is corrected to agree with the existing Korpelevich definition. Averaged iterates are introduced as analysis and evaluation quantities.

E1.justification: The experiments retain the same synthetic noisy polynomial-game family. Figure labels change the tested p values from {2.5, 3, 6} to {1.5, 2.5, 4, 6}, revising coverage of operator regimes. However, v2's prose still lists the original cases; its general R^(2d) formulation also does not specify the dimension actually tested.

E2.justification: The four-method comparator roster is retained. However, Section 5 changes the reported Popov clipping description: v1 specifies sample-based clipping analogous to Korpelevich, whereas v2 gives a rule involving the exact operator norm and an additional iterate-displacement term. This revises the described comparator without establishing what implementation changed.

E3.justification: The plotted iteration horizon increases from 1,000 to 20,000. V2 adds evaluation of beta-weighted averaged iterates alongside current iterates, substantially changing the evaluation design. The former larger-initial-stepsize setting, beta_k = 50/(10 + k^(1-epsilon)), is removed.

E4.justification: V1's Figure 3 tests robustness to a larger initial stepsize. V2 removes that analysis and introduces Figures 3–4 comparing weighted-average behavior under two decay exponents. This adds a substantive investigation of how averaging changes the preferred stepsize decay and relative method performance.

E5.justification: Both versions describe averaging experimental distances over twenty runs. Neither introduces confidence intervals, significance tests, seed specifications, or another empirical uncertainty-reporting practice. The new martingale variance calculations belong to the theoretical analysis.

E6.justification: The experimental curves are replaced or extended under revised horizons and parameter cases, and averaged-iterate results are added. V2 reports that smaller q benefits averaged iterates and that the projection variants outperform Korpelevich on that measure, while larger q benefits current iterates near the noise neighborhood. These are newly reported findings, not established same-setting improvements over v1.

T1.justification: V2 substantially revises Lemmas 3.1 and 4.1 and adds Lemmas B.1 and C.2 with martingale arguments for almost-sure divergence of the actual stepsize sum, replacing arguments about conditional expected stepsizes. Theorems 3.4 and 4.4 and their appendix proofs replace best-iterate quantities with weighted averages and state the averaging case for p >= 2. Equation (2) also revises the generalized-smoothness definition.

C1.justification: The principal almost-sure convergence claims and rate orders remain. V2 makes the existing alpha <= 1/2 rate restriction explicit in the abstract, emphasizes unbiased convergence, and adds averaged-iterate guarantees to the conclusion and Table 1. The contribution statements also change from conditional-mean stepsize nonsummability to actual stepsize nonsummability.

C2.justification: V2 adds explanations for the similar empirical behavior of one- and two-sample projection, conjecturing that clipping bias is dominated by the progress term. It also explains why clipping removes Korpelevich's usual stepsize advantage and distinguishes current-iterate from averaged-iterate preferences for q. The principal open questions concerning alpha > 1/2 and weaker sharpness assumptions remain.

D1.justification: V2 supplies explicit Popov recurrences and clipping details previously described only by analogy, an underlying min-max formulation for the synthetic operator, and the weighted-averaging calculation. These improve procedural documentation, although the actual dimension and conflicting experimental parameter lists remain unresolved.

R1.justification: V2 substantially expands research positioning through quantitative comparisons with smooth SGDA and extragradient guarantees, connections to deterministic results, and discussion of optimal dependence on the sharpness parameter. It also refines the comparison with Xian et al. and adds literature connecting quasi-sharpness to error bounds, other operator classes, and applications.

P1.justification: The six main sections and Appendices A–C retain their organization. V2 edits terminology, grammar, and section titles, expands explanations around assumptions and convergence arguments, rewrites parts of the experimental discussion, and adds acknowledgments. The narrative is refined without wholesale restructuring.

P2.justification: The experimental displays are reorganized from three-panel to four-panel figures, with extended axes and new averaged-iterate figures replacing the initial-stepsize display. Table 1 adds explicit alpha ranges and changes its explanatory caption. A different document template also changes typography, headings, author presentation, and page layout throughout.

improvement.justification: V2 adds useful averaged-iterate analysis, longer experiments, and clearer research positioning, but the theoretical revision introduces a material concern. Unlike v1, Appendix B.1 Equation (42) conditions on the clipping sample while retaining a variance bound for its now-fixed error, which Assumption 2.5 does not justify. The new experimental panels also conflict with the retained parameter list. These issues prevent a reliable net quality judgment despite the added analysis and explanation.
